newsitem.title: JAPAN: Baht move buoys yen on flight-to-quality factor.
newsitem.headline: Baht move buoys yen on flight-to-quality factor.

text.p: The surprise move to float the Thai baht on Wednesday sent funds flowing towards the relative safety of the yen, buoying the Japanese currency against the dollar.

The de-facto devaluation of the baht by Thailand's central bank unleashed a wave of speculative purchases as traders bet that investors worried about vulnerable Southeast Asian currencies would scurry to the yen as a safe haven.

Traders said institutional investors would likely cut their exposure to Thailand in light of its renewed currency woes, but that the impact of the "flight to quality" factor may be muted in the longer term.
"The Japanese currency could be among the beneficiaries of the baht woes due to flight-to-quality buying from Southeast Asian currencies," said a senior trader at a major Japanese bank in Tokyo.
The Bank of Thailand (BOT) announced on Wednesday it had switched to a "managed float" policy on the baht, and also raised interest rates to try to shore up the battered currency.

"The Thai baht will not get a free lunch from being fixed against a basket of currencies any more," said a currency analyst at a major U.S. bank in Tokyo, referring to the previous pegged-rate system.
The move pushed the dollar down as low as 114.15 yen and 1.7435 marks, compared with a New York close of around 114.92 yen and 1.7470 marks on Tuesday.
The news sent a shock wave through Asian foreign exchange markets but traders said that in the longer term the impact on major units such as the dollar and the yen would be limited.

"The spillover impact on major currencies such as the dollar and the yen is unlikely to be significant in the long run," said Toshihiko Masaki, senior trader at the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan (LTCB).
Tokyo dealers said the Thai baht fell as low as 29.25 against the dollar in response to the flotation announcement. At 0648 GMT, it stood at around 28.75 to the dollar.
"The BOT announcement is a 'de facto' devaluation of its currency. This suggests more of a burden on the country in the repayment of external debts," the senior bank trader said.

Thailand holds a massive 12.935 trillion yen ($112 billion) in yen-denominated loans from the Japanese government as of the end of March, 1996. A weaker baht means the Thai government needs to raise more money to pay back the yen debt to Tokyo.
"Certainly, the BOT will try to defend its currency as a weaker baht will push them to the verge of not meeting their international obligations on debt payment," said LTCB's Masaki.

Thai central bank Governor Rerngchai Marakanond said on Wednesday that the Bank of Thailand had an "appropriate rate" in mind for the baht and would intervene in the market if the currency strayed from that level.

As for Japanese investors' attitude, traders said that institutional investors would further reduce their exposure to Thailand. Holdings of Thai stocks and bonds by Japanese investment trusts totalled 93.14 billion yen ($809 million) as of the end of April, the latest figure available. This was down sharply from 121.95 billion yen ($1.06 billion) at the end of August, 1996.

"The baht was already said to be overvalued, given the current Thai economy. So the baht's movement will mirror Thai economic conditions," said Ken Kawai, manager at the foreign exchange and treasury division of the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
"This news means that the central bank will not offer a fixing rate, so it is essentially a float system...Without giving the fixing rate, a wide range of fluctuation will be allowed," he added.

Currencies such as the Philippine peso and Malaysian ringgit are likely to be exposed to strong downward pressure after the baht's tumble. The Philippine peso was hit by fallout from the Thai announcement and the Philippine central bank raised interest rates to counter speculative attacks.
"The Philippine peso is also seen as overvalued. It may be sold in reaction to the news (from Thailand)," said the analyst at a U.S. bank. ($1=115 yen)
